patterns_data.top_pattern: Authorization and facility mapping issues are distorting inpatient and post-acute spend signals
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: PPO Local and Medicare GRS inpatient and post-acute claims tied to authorization status and facility classification
key_driver_codes: Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: Before taking utilization or network action, the plan needs to validate how authorization status and facility type are being assigned on claims. A large share of the increase sits in authorization-code redistribution and Not Mapped facility buckets across GA, CA, ME / NY / OH, and CT / NH / NY / OH. That means some apparent provider, site-of-care, or authorization trends may be classification movement rather than true operating change.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: If these records are misclassified, the business could chase the wrong utilization, provider, or reimbursement lever.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a targeted audit of auth-to-claim mapping and facility taxonomy for the cited states and providers, restate the impacted claims, and only then route residual confirmed change to UM, reimbursement, and network teams.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The increase is explicitly tied to authorization-code movement and unmapped facility buckets, so business action should wait until mapping is confirmed.
evidence_summary: GA authorization-code movement added about $2.2M, led by Aftercare with CC/MCC at about $1.3M and Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC at about $0.9M.
CA authorization-code movement added about $0.9M in Miscellaneous Disorders of Nutrition, Metabolism, and Fluids and Electrolytes with MCC.
Not Mapped facility claims added about $0.3M in CA, about $0.3M in GA, and about $0.3M across CT / NH / NY / OH, with concentration at Good Samaritan Hospital and AdventHealth Palm Coast Parkway.

patterns_data.top_pattern: CA spend is rising in acute hospital and rehab settings, concentrated in aftercare, electrolyte, trauma, and spine cases
patterns_data.what_is_impacting: CA PPO Local acute hospital and physical rehab admissions
key_driver_codes: Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC
Miscellaneous Disorders of Nutrition, Metabolism, and Fluids and Electrolytes with MCC
patterns_data.pattern_details: CA has a concentrated inpatient and post-acute cost increase across PPO Local acute hospital and physical rehab settings. The operational increase is reinforced by clinical concentration in aftercare, electrolyte disorders, and a smaller set of rare trauma and spine cases, with Good Samaritan Hospital appearing repeatedly. This looks less like broad-based inflation and more like a focused mix of placement, case complexity, and provider concentration.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: CA has enough scale and concentration to support joint UM, clinical, and network action rather than a broad statewide policy change.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Launch a joint CA review of aftercare and electrolyte admissions, validate whether rehab placement was appropriate, and assess provider-specific pricing and episode management at Good Samaritan Hospital.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Part of the CA increase includes rare small-count cases and an unmapped clinical bucket, so confirm coding and episode classification while reviewing placement and reimbursement.
evidence_summary: CA physical rehab added about $0.7M in mixed volume and unit-cost pressure, including 10 more admissions and about $16.0K higher paid per admit in Aftercare with CC/MCC.

CA acute hospital added about $0.8M in mixed and volume-led pressure, led by Aftercare, Musculoskeletal System and Connective Tissue with CC at about $0.3M and Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC at about $0.2M.
Clinical case mix added about $0.9M from aftercare and electrolyte diagnoses, including ENC AFTERCARE FLW SURGERY NEOPLASM at about $0.3M and HYPO-OSMOLALITY AND HYPONATREMIA at about $0.2M.
Rare trauma and spine-related cases added about $0.9M, including several single-case episodes paid at roughly $40K to $175K per admit.

patterns_data.pattern_details: GA shows a focused rise in PPO Local acute hospital and rehab spend, with acute hospital pressure led by cellulitis and UTI admissions and rehab pressure tied to aftercare. The clinical signal is concentrated in UTI, cystitis, and lower-limb cellulitis diagnoses rather than broad inpatient growth. This points to a manageable set of admission and discharge pathways, with some provider concentration also appearing at Emory Hospital Perry.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: GA offers a clear opportunity to reduce spend through tighter admission management and better post-acute routing for recurring medical and aftercare episodes.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Review GA admission criteria and discharge routing for UTI, cellulitis, and aftercare cases, then assess whether provider-specific reimbursement or transfer patterns are amplifying the increase.
evidence_summary: GA acute hospital added about $0.7M, led by Cellulitis without MCC at about $0.3M and Kidney and Urinary Tract Infections without MCC at about $0.2M, with 68 more admissions across those two drivers.
GA clinical concentration added about $1.0M, led by UTI SITE NOT SPECIFIED at about $0.4M and lower-limb cellulitis diagnoses at about $0.3M combined.
GA physical rehab added about $0.3M across aftercare episodes, including 9 more admissions and higher paid per admit in the largest rehab cells.

patterns_data.what_is_impacting: Rare inpatient cases and unusual diagnoses across OH, GA / NY, CA / NY, CA / GA, and GA / NY / OH

Degenerative Nervous System Disorders without MCC

patterns_data.pattern_details: The remaining clinical increase is concentrated in rare, high-cost episodes rather than broad condition trends. Examples include sepsis with O.R. procedures, degenerative neurologic disorders, hip and femur fracture procedures, and isolated respiratory infections, often with only 1 to 2 admissions but very high paid per admit. These are better handled as targeted case reviews and possible catastrophic-event management than as systemwide utilization growth.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Treating rare outliers like broad trend changes would misdirect policy and operational resources.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Send the cited rare episodes to focused clinical review and data-quality audit to confirm diagnosis and DRG assignment, case severity, and any stop-loss or case-management opportunity.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Most of these cases are low-count, high-cost outliers, so coding and case classification should be confirmed before broad action.
evidence_summary: OH rare high-cost cases added about $0.3M, including femur fracture and pathologic vertebral fracture episodes paid at roughly $27K to $72K per admit.
CA / NY sepsis O.R. cases added about $0.1M, led by Good Samaritan Hospital at about $0.1M on 2 admissions.
GA / NY rare hip, bowel, cardiac, and respiratory cases added about $0.2M, mostly from 1 to 2 admission events.
GA / NY / OH septicemia without prolonged ventilation added about $53K across 4 single-admission cases.
